analysis.one_liner: Lets workers form a union by signing majority cards instead of winning an election, and speeds up first union contracts.
analysis.headline: The Workplace Democracy Act never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed how workers form unions under the National Labor Relations Act. If a majority of workers at a workplace signed cards saying they wanted a union, the National Labor Relations Board would have to certify the union directly, skipping the employer-requested election that employers can use to campaign against unionization. It would also set hard deadlines for negotiating a first union contract: bargaining would have to start within 10 days, a federal mediator could be called in after 90 days, and if mediation failed after 30 more days, an arbitrator would impose a binding two-year contract. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Workers trying to organize would benefit most. Today, after workers sign union cards, employers can demand a secret-ballot election and use the months before it to run anti-union campaigns; this bill would let a majority of signed cards itself establish the union. Workers at newly organized shops would also benefit from the first-contract deadlines, which address the common problem of employers negotiating slowly for years so that the union never gets a contract. Labor unions would gain members and bargaining leverage. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: A majority of employees signing valid authorization cards would be enough for the NLRB to certify the union without holding an election, removing the delay and employer campaigning that elections currently allow. [S2] [S3]

First contracts could not drag on indefinitely: bargaining would have to begin within 10 days, either side could call in a federal mediator after 90 days, and unresolved disputes would go to binding arbitration that sets a two-year contract. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear the cost. Companies that currently resist unionization through election campaigns and slow first-contract bargaining would lose both tools, and binding first-contract arbitration would set wages and terms that employers could not veto. Business and employer associations opposed card-check proposals like this one, arguing workers should decide unions through secret ballots and that imposed contracts remove employer choice. [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: Union certification would no longer require a secret-ballot election, so workers would be deciding in a process where their choice is known to the employer and to co-workers, and where organizing committees or unions control which workers get asked to sign and when. Defenders of the current election system argue the private ballot is the fairest way to test majority support. [S2] [S3]

Binding first-contract arbitration hands wage and contract decisions to an arbitrator rather than the parties, which critics say can impose terms that neither workers nor the employer actually chose and may not fit the business's finances. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers wanting a union, the bill removes two of the biggest roadblocks in current law: the employer-controlled election window and indefinite first-contract stalls. The trade-offs are real — losing the secret ballot in certification and letting an arbitrator set contract terms — but the bill's core effect would be to make union formation substantially easier at employers' expense. It died without a hearing, so none of this was tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and later to a subcommittee, but the Republican-controlled committee never held a hearing or brought it up, and it died when the Congress ended. [S1] [S5]

narrative.text: Representative Mark Pocan introduced the Workplace Democracy Act in the House on October 6, 2015. [S1] [S5]
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, and on March 23, 2016 was referred to its Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions. [S1] [S5]
Thirty-eight House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did. [S4]
The committee took no further action — no markup, no hearing, no floor vote — and the bill expired at the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off: they keep the current system, in which a union can be signed up by a majority of workers but must then win an election the employer can request and campaign in, and in which first contracts can stall indefinitely with no penalty. Unions and workers seeking to organize gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Mark Pocan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Workplace Democracy Act and recruited 38 Democratic cosponsors. [S1] [S4]

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee (Republican-controlled)
against.role: Committee of referral; controlled whether the bill got a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — sending it to a subcommittee in March 2016 and letting it die there. [S5]

against.name: 246 of 246 House Republicans
against.role: House majority; none cosponsored, and their committee leadership buried the bill
against.what_they_did: Provided no support for the bill and controlled the committee process that kept it from a vote. [S4]

against.name: Business and employer associations
against.what_they_did: Long opposed card-check and mandatory first-contract arbitration proposals like this one, which would remove the election requirement and impose contracts by arbitration.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat (38 of 188 House Democrats plus the sponsor); no Republican signed on, and the Republican-led committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Card-check certification and first-contract deadlines would make organizing far easier and grow union membership and bargaining power; for workers, that means a shorter path to a contract covering their workplace. [S2] [S3]

Employers would lose the ability to demand an election and campaign against a union after workers had already signed majority cards, and would face binding arbitration on first contracts. These levers are how many workplaces stay non-union. [S2] [S3]
